metrics.title: Inflation
metrics.question: Is inflation back inside the Reserve Bank's 2–3% target band?

headline.caption: annual CPI inflation, measured over the past 12 months

metrics.status_rule: On track if the latest annual CPI inflation rate is within the RBA's 2–3% target band; otherwise off track.
context: Prices overall are 16.8% higher than in the June quarter 2022.
On the quarterly measure, inflation has been above the top of the 2–3% target band in 13 of the 17 quarters since the government took office. It was 3.9% in the June quarter 2026.
Underlying (trimmed mean) inflation, which strips out volatile items, was 3.6% in the June quarter 2026.
Inflation was already 6.2% in the June quarter 2022 when the government took office. The test is how quickly it has come back down, and whether it has stayed down.

sources.title: Consumer Price Index, Australia
series: All groups CPI, weighted average of eight capital cities: monthly annual % change (headline) and index (cross-check); quarterly index (cross-check)

sources.title: Statistical Table G1 – Consumer Price Inflation

metrics.method: Headline: the ABS monthly Consumer Price Index, percentage change from the same month a year earlier (all groups, eight capitals). History: year-ended quarterly CPI inflation from RBA Table G1, which extends back decades. The cumulative change compares the latest quarterly CPI index with the June quarter 2022.

explainer.what: Inflation is how fast prices are rising across a typical basket of goods and services: food, rent, petrol, power, insurance and more. The ABS measures it with the Consumer Price Index (CPI), and this figure compares prices with the same quarter a year earlier.
explainer.why: When inflation runs above wage growth, household budgets shrink. The Reserve Bank aims to keep inflation between 2% and 3% on average. Inflation above that band usually means higher interest rates.

metrics.title: Prices vs wages since the election
metrics.question: Have wages kept up with the cost of essentials?

headline.caption: of 8 essential price categories rose faster than wages

benchmark.label: Wages growth over the same period

metrics.status_rule: Off track if the overall price level has risen faster than wages since the June quarter 2022.
context: Wages (Wage Price Index) are up 15.1%; overall prices are up 16.8%.
Rising faster than wages: Insurance, Electricity, Rents, Education, Health, Food.
The ABS counts government energy bill rebates as a cut in electricity prices while they are paid, so the electricity figure is after taxpayer-funded rebates.

chart.note: Change in price index, June quarter 2022 to June quarter 2026. Bars crossing the blue line rose faster than wages.

sources.title: Consumer Price Index, Australia
series: Child care (index 115498), eight capital cities, original
Petrol & fuel (index 40081), eight capital cities, original
All prices (CPI) (index 10001), eight capital cities, original

sources.title: Wage Price Index, Australia
series: Total hourly rates of pay excluding bonuses; private and public; all industries; original

metrics.method: Percentage change in each ABS CPI expenditure-class index and the Wage Price Index between the June quarter 2022 and the latest quarter available for all series.

explainer.what: This compares how much the prices of everyday essentials have risen since mid-2022 with how much wages have risen. Wages are measured by the ABS Wage Price Index, which tracks pay for the same jobs over time.
explainer.why: If the things you must buy rise faster than your pay, you are worse off even if your pay rose. It shows where the squeeze on households is coming from.

metrics.title: Real wages: private vs public sector
metrics.question: Can a worker's pay buy more than it could when the government took office, and has the private sector done as well as government employees?

headline.caption: change in private-sector real wages since June quarter 2022

metrics.status_rule: Off track if private-sector wages adjusted for inflation are below their June quarter 2022 level; watch if they have grown less than public-sector real wages.
context: Private sector: real wages −1.4%. Public sector: −1.8%. All workers: −1.5%.
Latest year: private wages +3.1%, public wages +3.4%, prices +3.9%. Real wage growth is private −0.8 and public −0.5 percentage points.
Across all workers, wages grew more slowly than prices in 9 of the 17 quarters since the government took office.
All-worker real wages are 6.7% below their pre-election peak on this measure.
The Treasurer's own release on 19 August 2026 acknowledged real wages fell by 0.8% over the year (unrounded).

ref.label: Level when the government took office

sources.title: Wage Price Index, Australia
series: Total hourly rates of pay excluding bonuses; private sector, public sector and all sectors; all industries; original

sources.title: Consumer Price Index, Australia
series: All groups CPI index, eight capitals

sources.title: Statistical Table H4 – Labour Costs and Productivity
Statistical Table G1 – Consumer Price Inflation
Media release: wages continue to grow under Labor (19 August 2026)

metrics.method: ABS Wage Price Index (by sector) divided by the Consumer Price Index, rebased so the June quarter 2022 = 100. A value below 100 means pay buys less than it did then. Year-ended wage growth by sector from RBA Table H4.

explainer.what: 'Real' wages are wages adjusted for inflation: what your pay can actually buy. We divide the Wage Price Index by the Consumer Price Index and set mid-2022 to 100. Below 100 means pay buys less than it did then. Private-sector and public-sector workers are shown separately.
explainer.why: A pay rise is only a real gain if it beats inflation. The sector split shows whether workers in private business have fared differently from government employees.

metrics.title: Electricity prices
metrics.question: Did power bills come down, as promised?

headline.caption: change in electricity prices since June quarter 2022

metrics.status_rule: Off track if household electricity prices are higher than in the June quarter 2022.
context: Overall prices rose 16.8% over the same period.
The ABS measures electricity prices after government energy bill rebates. While rebates are paid they lower the measured price, but taxpayers still fund them.
ABS monthly CPI: electricity prices rose 21.1% in the 12 months to May 2026, or 3.9% excluding the effect of Commonwealth and state bill rebates, which were winding down.

sources.title: Promise check: cut power bills by $275

metrics.method: ABS CPI electricity index and all-groups index, each rebased so the June quarter 2022 = 100.

explainer.what: The change in household electricity prices recorded in the Consumer Price Index since the June quarter 2022, shown next to overall inflation. The ABS counts government bill rebates as a price reduction while they are paid.
explainer.why: Power bills hit every household and business. Before the 2022 election, lower power bills were a central promise.

promise.quote: It will cut power bills … by $275 a year for homes by 2025, compared to today.
promise.attribution: Labor's Powering Australia plan announcement, 3 December 2021.

metrics.title: Power bills: the $275 promise
metrics.question: Did household power bills fall by $275 as promised?

headline.caption: a year: rise in the default power price for a typical NSW household (Ausgrid)

metrics.status_rule: Off track if the regulated default electricity offer in each benchmark region is higher, not $275 lower, than when the promise was made.
context: Default Market Offer, 2022–23 to 2026–27: NSW (Ausgrid) $1,512 → $1,899; South-East Queensland (Energex) $1,620 → $1,988; South Australia $1,840 → $2,334.
Victorian Default Offer: $1,403 → $1,591 over the same period.
The default offers are price caps on standing offers set by regulators for a typical household. Many households are on cheaper market offers, and the caps don't include government rebates.

promise.quote: It will cut power bills … by $275 a year for homes by 2025, compared to today.
promise.attribution: Labor's Powering Australia plan announcement, 3 December 2021. Source: RMIT ABC Fact Check and Labor media release.

chart.note: Change in annual default electricity offer, 2022–23 to 2026–27 ($ a year, incl. GST), compared with the promised $275 cut.

sources.title: Default Market Offer prices 2026–27: final determination
Default Market Offer price determination 2022–23: final determination
Promise check: cut power bills by $275

metrics.method: Annual bill at benchmark usage for residential customers on a flat tariff without controlled load (GST inclusive), from the regulators' final determinations. Change = 2026–27 minus 2022–23.

explainer.what: Each year energy regulators set a 'default offer', a maximum price for households on standard electricity contracts, based on typical usage in each region. It is the most consistent official yardstick for what a typical power bill costs.
explainer.why: Before the 2022 election, Labor promised its energy plan would cut household power bills by $275 a year by 2025. The regulators' own numbers show whether that happened.

metrics.title: Wholesale gas prices
metrics.question: Have east-coast wholesale gas prices come down from the 2022 crisis?

headline.caption: average east-coast wholesale gas price

metrics.status_rule: On track if the average east-coast wholesale gas price is below its June quarter 2022 level.
context: Wholesale gas prices hit a record $28.40/GJ in the June quarter 2022 during the global energy crisis after Russia invaded Ukraine. They have since fallen to $9.08/GJ, the lowest since mid-2021.
A temporary $12/GJ emergency price cap was introduced from 23 December 2022.
The ACCC says long-term contract prices are around $13–15/GJ, which is what many businesses pay. Lower wholesale gas has not flowed through to lower electricity bills (see the $275 promise).

chart.note: Selected quarters reported by AEMO Quarterly Energy Dynamics.

sources.title: Storage vital to meeting winter demand across east coast gas market in Q3 2026

metrics.method: Average east-coast wholesale gas price for the quarter as reported in AEMO's Quarterly Energy Dynamics.

explainer.what: The average price of gas traded in east-coast wholesale markets, in dollars per gigajoule. It is a key input cost for manufacturers, gas-fired power stations and household gas bills.
explainer.why: We report the good news too. Wholesale gas has fallen sharply from its 2022 peak, but households haven't seen that in their electricity bills.

metrics.title: Emissions target
metrics.question: Is Australia on track for the government's legislated 43% emissions cut by 2030?

headline.caption: below 2005 emissions levels

metrics.status_rule: Off track if the government's own latest projections show the 2030 target will not be met.
context: Emissions were 455.6 million tonnes CO2-e in the year to March 2026, 25.0% below 2005 levels.
The government's 2025 Annual Climate Change Statement projects a 42% reduction by 2030, short of the 43% target it legislated.

chart.note: Reduction below 2005 emissions levels. A land-sector recalculation in 2026 lowered reported reductions, so don't compare this with figures published earlier.

sources.publisher: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
sources.title: Quarterly Update of Australia's National Greenhouse Gas Inventory: March 2026

sources.publisher: Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
sources.title: Annual Climate Change Statement 2025

metrics.method: National inventory emissions (year to March 2026) compared with 2005, and the government's published 2030 projection.

explainer.what: Australia's total greenhouse gas emissions compared with 2005 levels, from the official national inventory. The Climate Change Act 2022 sets a target of a 43% reduction by 2030.
explainer.why: It is the government's own legislated target, and it has justified energy policy and spending decisions by it. Missing it on its own projections is a test of delivery.

metrics.title: Mortgage costs
metrics.question: How much more are households paying on a typical mortgage?

headline.caption: extra per month on a $600,000 loan vs May 2022

metrics.status_rule: Off track if repayments on a typical variable mortgage are higher than in May 2022.
context: The average variable rate on existing owner-occupier loans is 6.20%, up from 3.10% in May 2022.
That is about $13,353 a year more on a $600,000, 30-year principal-and-interest loan.
The RBA cash rate is 4.35%. The RBA sets rates independently to control inflation, and government spending adds to demand and inflation.

sources.title: Statistical Table F6 – Housing Lending Rates
Statistical Table F1.1 – Interest Rates and Yields – Money Market

metrics.method: Standard amortisation formula applied to a $600,000 30-year principal-and-interest loan, using the RBA's average rate on outstanding owner-occupier variable loans in May 2022 and the latest month.

explainer.what: The average interest rate on existing variable home loans for owner-occupiers (RBA data), and what that means in monthly repayments on a typical $600,000, 30-year loan compared with May 2022.
explainer.why: About a third of Australian households are paying off a mortgage. Higher repayments take money directly out of their budgets.

metrics.title: Interest rate rises
metrics.question: How many times have interest rates gone up under this government?

headline.caption: cash rate rises, versus 3 cuts

benchmark.label: Cash rate when government was sworn in

metrics.status_rule: Off track if the cash rate is higher than on the day the government was sworn in.
context: The cash rate is 4.35%, up 4.00 percentage points from 0.35% when the government was sworn in.
There have been 15 rises and 3 cuts since then, including 3 rises so far in 2026.
The RBA sets the cash rate independently. It raises rates when inflation is too high, and government spending adds to demand in the economy.

sources.title: Statistical Table F1.1 – Interest Rates and Yields – Money Market
Statistical Table A2 – Changes in Monetary Policy and Administered Rates

metrics.method: Every cash rate target decision published in RBA Table A2 after 23 May 2022, cross-checked against the monthly cash rate target in Table F1.1.

explainer.what: The cash rate is the Reserve Bank's official interest rate. Banks base their lending rates on it. This counts every decision to raise or cut it since the government was sworn in on 23 May 2022.
explainer.why: The RBA is independent, but it raises rates when inflation is too high, and government spending affects inflation. At current rates, each 0.25-point rise adds about $100 a month to repayments on a $600,000 loan.

metrics.title: Housing Accord: 1.2 million homes
metrics.question: Is the government on track to build 1.2 million new homes in five years from July 2024?

headline.caption: of the required pace achieved

metrics.status_rule: Off track if cumulative completions since July 2024 are more than 5% behind the 60,000-a-quarter pace needed; watch if behind at all.
context: 306,383 homes completed in 7 quarters, against 420,000 needed to stay on pace: a shortfall of 113,617.
To reach 1.2 million, completions would now need to average 68,740 a quarter for the remaining 13 quarters.
Latest quarter: 38,182 completions and 45,154 commencements.

The government's own advisory body, the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council, counts 308,000 completions (about 26% of the target) after 7 of 20 quarters. It expects 1.2 million to be reached only in the December quarter 2030, 18 months after the Accord ends.

sources.title: Building Activity, Australia
series: Dwelling units completed, new residential, all sectors, Australia, original

sources.publisher: National Housing Supply and Affordability Council
sources.title: Quarterly report, August 2026

metrics.method: Sum of ABS new residential dwelling completions (original series) from the September quarter 2024 (the Accord began 1 July 2024) to the latest quarter, compared with 1.2 million ÷ 20 quarters = 60,000 per quarter.

explainer.what: Under the National Housing Accord, federal and state governments committed to 1.2 million new homes in the five years from 1 July 2024. That is 60,000 a quarter. We add up ABS new dwelling completions since then.
explainer.why: It is the government's own target. Falling behind means rents and prices stay under pressure, especially while population growth is strong.

metrics.title: Home prices
metrics.question: Is home ownership getting further out of reach?

headline.caption: average price of a residential dwelling in Australia

metrics.status_rule: Off track if average dwelling prices have risen faster than wages since the June quarter 2022.
context: The average dwelling price is up 19.5% ($179,200) since the June quarter 2022, while wages rose 15.1%.
Homes are less affordable for first-home buyers relying on wages.

sources.title: Total Value of Dwellings
series: Mean price of residential dwellings, Australia

metrics.method: ABS Total Value of Dwellings: mean price of residential dwellings (total value of dwelling stock ÷ number of dwellings). Compared with the Wage Price Index over the same period.

explainer.what: The ABS calculates the average price of a residential dwelling by dividing the total value of all homes by the number of homes. We compare its growth since mid-2022 with wage growth.
explainer.why: When home prices grow faster than wages, saving a deposit and paying off a mortgage takes longer. Home ownership moves out of reach for younger Australians.

metrics.title: Unemployment
metrics.question: Are more Australians out of work than when the government took office?

headline.caption: unemployment rate

metrics.status_rule: Off track if the unemployment rate is higher than in May 2022.
context: 137,900 more Australians are unemployed than in May 2022.
Job growth has been concentrated in publicly funded sectors (see Who is creating the jobs?).

sources.title: Labour Force, Australia
series: Unemployment rate, persons, seasonally adjusted (independent cross-check)

metrics.method: Seasonally adjusted unemployment rate from the ABS Labour Force survey (via RBA Table H5), cross-checked against the ABS Data API.

explainer.what: The share of people in the labour force (working or actively looking for work) who do not have a job, from the ABS Labour Force Survey of about 50,000 people each month. Seasonally adjusted.
explainer.why: It is the most-watched measure of whether the economy is providing enough work. It doesn't show underemployment (people who want more hours) or what kind of jobs are being created.

metrics.title: Public vs private sector jobs
metrics.question: Are government jobs growing faster than jobs in private business?

headline.caption: growth in public-sector jobs

metrics.status_rule: Off track if public-sector jobs have grown more than 1.25× as fast as private-sector jobs since June quarter 2022; watch if faster at all.
context: Public-sector filled jobs rose by 237,000 (+10.9%). Private-sector jobs rose by 1,222,000 (+9.6%).
The public sector made up 14.6% of jobs in June quarter 2022 but 16.2% of the jobs added since.
Many jobs funded by government, such as NDIS disability support workers and aged-care workers, are counted as private-sector jobs. See 'Who is creating the jobs?' for the industry picture.

sources.title: Labour Account Australia (quarterly)
series: Filled jobs – public sector (M14), private sector (M13) and total (M12); all industries; seasonally adjusted

metrics.method: ABS Labour Account filled jobs by institutional sector (public = all levels of government and public corporations), seasonally adjusted. Growth measured from the June quarter 2022.

explainer.what: The ABS Labour Account counts filled jobs and classifies each employer as public sector (federal, state and local government and government-owned businesses) or private sector. This compares how fast each has grown since mid-2022.
explainer.why: Private businesses fund the tax base. If government employment grows faster than private employment, more of the economy depends on taxpayers.

metrics.title: Who is creating the jobs?
metrics.question: Is employment growth coming from the private economy or from taxpayer-funded sectors?

headline.caption: of all new jobs were in health & social assistance (incl. NDIS), education and public administration

benchmark.label: Those sectors' share of all jobs in June qtr 2022

metrics.status_rule: Off track if these largely publicly funded industries account for more than 1.5× their share of jobs in new jobs; watch if above their share.
context: Filled jobs grew by 1,445,000. 756,000 of them were in health care & social assistance, education and public administration. Health care & social assistance alone added 453,000.
Those three industries held 27.3% of jobs in June quarter 2022. The other 16 industries, mostly the market economy, added 689,000.

Economists call these three industries the 'non-market' sector because they are largely government funded. They include some private employers (such as private hospitals and schools), so this is not a pure public-sector count. See 'Public vs private sector jobs' for that.
The Reserve Bank reported in November 2024 that around three-quarters of employment growth over the preceding year was in the non-market parts of the economy.

chart.note: Change in filled jobs by industry ('000), June quarter 2022 to June quarter 2026, seasonally adjusted. Highlighted: largely publicly funded industries.

sources.title: Labour Account Australia (quarterly)
series: Filled jobs (M12) by ANZSIC industry division, seasonally adjusted, quarterly

sources.title: Statement on Monetary Policy, November 2024, Box D

metrics.method: Change in ABS Labour Account filled jobs in each of the 19 ANZSIC industry divisions between the June quarter 2022 and the latest quarter. 'Non-market' = Health Care & Social Assistance + Education & Training + Public Administration & Safety. (The ABS ceased the Labour Force, Detailed industry tables in April 2026; the Labour Account is the continuing official quarterly source.)

explainer.what: Change in filled jobs in each of the 19 major industries since mid-2022. Health care & social assistance (which includes NDIS and aged care), education, and public administration are highlighted. Economists call these the 'non-market' sector because they are mostly paid for by government.
explainer.why: Headline job numbers can look strong even when growth relies on government-funded programs rather than a thriving private economy. This shows where the jobs are actually coming from.

metrics.title: Productivity
metrics.question: Are we producing more for every hour worked? Productivity drives lasting wage growth.

headline.caption: average annual productivity growth since the government took office

metrics.status_rule: Off track if annual productivity growth since June quarter 2022 is below the 2000–2019 average.
context: Output per hour worked in the non-farm economy is 3.4% below its June quarter 2022 level.
Over the latest year productivity changed by −0.3%.

Measured productivity was temporarily lifted during the COVID period, so the June 2022 starting point was unusually high. Against the pre-COVID December quarter 2019, productivity is 1.1% lower: an average of −0.17% a year, still below the long-run +1.17%.
Without productivity growth, real wages cannot rise sustainably.
Productivity Commission, June 2026: labour productivity fell 0.6% in the March quarter and grew only 0.3% over the year.

sources.title: Statistical Table H4 – Labour Costs and Productivity

metrics.method: ABS national accounts non-farm GDP per hour worked (RBA Table H4). Annualised growth rates are compound averages between the quarters shown.

explainer.what: Labour productivity is how much the economy produces for each hour worked, measured here for the non-farm economy in the ABS national accounts. We compare average annual growth since mid-2022 with the 2000–2019 average.
explainer.why: Productivity is the only lasting way to raise wages and living standards. The Productivity Commission and RBA have both warned that weak productivity growth holds back real incomes.

metrics.title: Business collapses
metrics.question: Are more businesses going under?

headline.caption: companies entering external administration for the first time

metrics.status_rule: Off track if company insolvencies are above the pre-COVID 2018–19 level.
context: Insolvencies rose from 4,912 in 2021–22 to 7,942, then 11,053, then 14,722 in 2024–25, 82% above the pre-COVID level.
2020–21 and 2021–22 were unusually low because of temporary COVID insolvency relief, so we compare with 2018–19.
ASIC recorded 12,819 in the first 11 months of 2025–26 (to 31 May 2026).
metrics.method: ASIC Series 1: companies entering external administration or having a controller appointed for the first time, by financial year.

explainer.what: The number of companies entering formal insolvency (administration, liquidation or receivership) for the first time each year, as recorded by the corporate regulator ASIC.
explainer.why: Business failures mean lost jobs, unpaid suppliers and owners losing their livelihoods. A sustained rise is a warning sign about costs, tax debts and the health of small business.

metrics.title: Consumer confidence
metrics.question: Do Australians feel confident about their finances and the economy?

headline.caption: consumer sentiment index (100 = optimists equal pessimists)

metrics.status_rule: Off track if pessimists outnumber optimists (index below 100).
context: Pessimists have outnumbered optimists in 51 of the 52 months since the government took office.
In May 2022 the index was 90.4. The 2010–2019 average was 101.2.

sources.title: Statistical Table H3 – Monthly Activity Indicators
sources.note: Index compiled by Westpac Banking Corporation and the Melbourne Institute; republished by the RBA in Table H3.

metrics.method: Westpac–Melbourne Institute Index of Consumer Sentiment, seasonally adjusted, as republished in RBA Table H3. An index above 100 means more consumers are optimistic than pessimistic.

explainer.what: The Westpac–Melbourne Institute survey asks around 1,200 Australian adults each month how they feel about their family finances and the economy. 100 means optimists and pessimists are evenly balanced. Below 100 means pessimists outnumber optimists.
explainer.why: Confidence shapes spending, hiring and investment. A long run below 100 is a clear sign that households feel worse off.

metrics.title: GDP per person
metrics.question: Is the economy growing for each Australian, or only because the population is growing?

headline.caption: annual growth in real GDP per person

metrics.status_rule: Off track if average annual per-person GDP growth since the election is below the 2010–2019 average.
context: Average growth since the government took office: +0.3% a year, compared with +1.0% in 2010–2019.
Per-person GDP was lower than a year earlier in 8 of the 16 quarterly readings since the election.
Total GDP grew 2.1% over the latest year. The gap is population growth.
The ABS confirmed GDP per person fell for seven consecutive quarters before growing 0.1% in the December quarter 2024.

series.name: Real GDP per capita, year-ended growth

sources.title: Statistical Table H1 – Gross Domestic Product and Income
Media release: Australian economy grew 0.6 per cent in December quarter (2024)

metrics.method: Year-ended growth in real (chain volume) GDP per capita, seasonally adjusted, ABS national accounts via RBA Table H1. Averages are simple means of quarterly year-ended readings.

explainer.what: Gross domestic product (the total value of everything the economy produces), adjusted for inflation and divided by the population. This figure is the change over the past year.
explainer.why: Total GDP can grow just because the population grows. GDP per person shows whether the economy is growing for each Australian. When it falls for two quarters in a row, it is often called a 'per capita recession'.

metrics.title: Household income per person
metrics.question: After tax and inflation, are households better off per person?

headline.caption: change in real disposable income per person since June quarter 2022

metrics.status_rule: Off track if real household disposable income per person is below its June quarter 2022 level.
context: That is about $61,570 a year per person after adjusting for inflation, compared with $62,479 in the June quarter 2022 (ABS chain-volume dollars).
Disposable income is what households have left after income tax and interest payments, adjusted for inflation.

series.name: Real household disposable income per person (June qtr 2022 = 100)

sources.title: Statistical Table H2 – Demand and Income

metrics.method: Real household disposable income ($m, chain volume, seasonally adjusted; RBA Table H2) divided by ABS estimated resident population, annualised (×4) and rebased to June quarter 2022 = 100. Limited to the latest quarter for which both series are available.

explainer.what: Real household disposable income is the income households have left after income tax and interest payments, adjusted for inflation. We divide it by the population and set mid-2022 to 100.
explainer.why: It is one of the most complete measures of whether the average person is better or worse off, because it includes the effects of tax, interest rates and prices.

metrics.title: GP bulk billing
metrics.question: Can Australians see a GP without paying?

headline.caption: of GP visits bulk billed

metrics.status_rule: Watch if the GP bulk billing rate is below the government's promised 90%.
context: The annual GP bulk billing rate fell from 88.3% in 2021–22 to 77.3% in 2023–24, then recovered to 80.9% in 2025–26. The 2021–22 rate was inflated by COVID-era mandatory bulk billing for some patients.
The average out-of-pocket cost for a GP visit that isn't bulk billed rose from $42.25 in 2021–22 to $55.25 in 2025–26.
The quarterly rate has recovered from a low of 75.6% in October 2023 to 84.1% in the June quarter 2026.

sources.publisher: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
sources.title: Medicare annual statistics: state and territory, 2009–10 to 2025–26
Strengthening Medicare: bulk billing on the up
Delivering bulk billing for all Australians

metrics.method: Share of non-referred GP attendances that were bulk billed, by financial year (Medicare statistics). Latest quarterly rate from the Health Minister's release.

explainer.what: The share of GP visits where the doctor bills Medicare directly, so the patient pays nothing out of pocket.
explainer.why: Cost is a barrier to seeing a doctor. When bulk billing falls, people delay care and end up in emergency departments. The government has promised 9 in 10 GP visits will be bulk billed by 2030.

metrics.title: Size of government in the economy
metrics.question: How much of the economy is now government spending and investment?

headline.caption: of the economy is public demand

metrics.status_rule: Off track if public demand's share of output is more than 1 percentage point above its 2000–2019 average; watch if above average.
context: Public demand (spending and investment by all levels of government) is 5.1 percentage points above its pre-COVID two-decade average.
In the June quarter 2022 it was 25.9%.
This includes state and local governments as well as the Commonwealth.

sources.title: Statistical Table H2 – Demand and Income

metrics.method: Public final demand as a share of real output, ABS national accounts via RBA Table H2.

explainer.what: Public demand is spending and investment by federal, state and local governments (such as salaries, services, infrastructure and defence) as a share of total economic output, from the ABS national accounts.
explainer.why: When government takes up a bigger share of the economy, it can crowd out private investment and add to inflation. We compare it with the two decades before COVID.

metrics.title: Gross government debt
metrics.question: Is the Commonwealth's debt going up or down?

headline.caption: gross debt: above $1 trillion for the first time

benchmark.label: When the government took office (30 June 2022)

metrics.status_rule: Off track if gross debt (in dollars) is forecast to be higher than at 30 June 2022.
context: At 30 June 2006 gross debt was $54.1 billion (5.4% of GDP). It reached $257.4 billion in 2012–13, $542.0 billion in 2018–19 and $895.3 billion (38.3% of GDP) at 30 June 2022, when this government took office.
It was $928.6 billion at 30 June 2025, the latest audited actual. The Budget forecasts $1,051 billion by June 2027 and $1,249 billion by June 2030: above $1 trillion for the first time.

AOFM's register shows $971.4 billion of Australian Government Securities on issue at 30 June 2026, compared with the Budget estimate of $982.0 billion. The official 2025–26 figure is confirmed in the Final Budget Outcome.
As a share of the economy, gross debt peaked at 39.1% of GDP in 2020–21 and fell to 33.4% in 2024–25. The Budget forecasts it rising again to peak at 35.8% in 2028–29.
Net debt is forecast to rise from $532.3 billion (2024–25) to $767.8 billion by 2029–30.

Share of GDP uses the GDP figures in the 2026–27 Budget. Actual years are cross-checked automatically every day against the AOFM register of securities on issue.

explainer.what: Gross debt is the face value of all bonds and Treasury notes the Commonwealth has issued and not yet repaid: the amount it must pay back to investors when they mature. It is a snapshot at 30 June each year. Net debt, a separate measure, subtracts certain financial assets the government holds.
explainer.why: Debt has to be serviced. Every dollar of interest is a dollar not spent on services or returned as tax cuts, and higher debt leaves less room to respond to the next crisis. The long view shows how debt has built up over two decades and where it is forecast to go.

metrics.title: Budget deficits
metrics.question: Is the government living within its means?

headline.caption: underlying cash balance: a deficit

metrics.status_rule: Off track if the government's own Budget forecasts a deficit for the current financial year.
context: The budget recorded surpluses in 2022–23 (+$22.1 billion) and 2023–24 (+$15.8 billion), then returned to deficit in 2024–25 (−$10.0 billion).
The 2026–27 Budget forecasts a deficit in every year of the forward estimates: −$28.3b, −$31.5b, −$31.0b, −$34.4b and −$25.3b from 2025–26 to 2029–30.
Tax receipts are forecast at 23.8% of GDP in 2026–27, up from 23.0% in 2021–22. The tax take is higher as a share of the economy, but payments have risen faster (see Government spending).

chart.note: Red = deficit. Lighter bars are Budget forecasts. 2021–22 was the final budget year of the previous government.

sources.title: Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 11 (Table 11.1: underlying cash balance; Table 11.3: tax receipts)

metrics.method: Underlying cash balance (general government sector) as published in Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Table 11.1. Years to 2024–25 are actuals; later years are estimates.

explainer.what: The underlying cash balance is the Commonwealth's headline budget result: cash receipts minus cash payments, excluding the Future Fund's investment earnings. A negative number is a deficit.
explainer.why: Deficits are funded by borrowing, which adds to debt and interest costs. Deficit spending also adds to demand at a time when the Reserve Bank is trying to bring inflation down.

metrics.title: Interest on government debt
metrics.question: How much are taxpayers paying just to service the debt?

headline.caption: interest payments in one year

metrics.status_rule: Off track if annual interest payments are higher than in 2021–22.
context: Interest payments are forecast to rise from $17.4 billion in 2021–22 to $29.6 billion in 2026–27 and $42.3 billion by 2029–30.
The Budget itself says interest payments are expected to peak at 1.6% of GDP in 2032–33.

In 2026–27 the government expects to spend more on public debt interest ($31.9 billion, accrual basis) than on transport and communication ($15.3 billion) and public order and safety ($9.7 billion) combined.

chart.note: Cash interest payments, general government sector. Lighter bars are Budget forecasts.

sources.title: Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 11 (Table 11.4: interest payments)
Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27 (Table 6.3: expenses by function; Table 6.17: other purposes)
Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 3: Fiscal Strategy and Outlook

metrics.method: Interest payments (cash) from Budget Paper No. 1 Table 11.4. The comparison with other spending uses accrual expenses by function (Tables 6.3 and 6.17), which is why public debt interest expense ($31.9b) differs from cash interest payments ($29.6b).

explainer.what: The interest the Commonwealth pays each year to the investors who hold its bonds. It rises when debt grows and when interest rates on new borrowing are higher.
explainer.why: Interest buys nothing: no hospitals, no defence, no tax relief. It is a direct cost of past and present deficits, and future taxpayers carry it.

metrics.title: Government spending
metrics.question: How big is Commonwealth spending compared with the economy?

headline.caption: of GDP spent by the Commonwealth

metrics.status_rule: Off track if Commonwealth payments as a share of GDP are above the pre-COVID 2018–19 level.
context: Payments are forecast at $829.6 billion in 2026–27, up from $616.3 billion in 2021–22.
Spending was 24.3% of GDP in 2022–23. It has risen every year since and is forecast at 26.8% in both 2026–27 and 2027–28.
The 2021–22 figure (26.4%) still included pandemic support. Before COVID, in 2018–19, spending was 24.5% of GDP.

chart.note: 2025–26 onward are Budget estimates. Financial years ending 30 June.

metrics.method: General government sector cash payments and tax receipts as a percentage of GDP, Budget Paper No. 1 2026–27, Statement 11.

explainer.what: Total Commonwealth cash payments (welfare, health, defence, grants to the states, interest and so on) as a share of Australia's GDP. Tax receipts are shown for comparison.
explainer.why: It shows the size of the federal government relative to the economy. When spending grows faster than the economy, it must be paid for with higher taxes, more debt, or both.

metrics.title: Size of the public service
metrics.question: How fast has the Canberra bureaucracy grown?

headline.caption: growth in Australian Public Service (APS) headcount

metrics.status_rule: Off track if APS headcount grew more than twice as fast as Australia's population over the same period; watch if faster at all.
context: The APS grew from 159,179 employees at 30 June 2022 to 198,529 at 30 June 2025: 39,350 more public servants.
Australia's population grew 6.1% over the same three years, so the APS grew about 4.0 times faster than the population it serves.
The Budget estimates the APS Average Staffing Level at 217,256 in 2026–27.
The government says about 13,200 of the new roles replaced external contractors and consultants, around one-third of the increase in staffing since 2022.

chart.note: Ongoing plus non-ongoing employees at 30 June each year.

sources.title: State of the Service Report 2024–25: APS workforce size and location (Table 10)
Budget Paper No. 4 2026–27: Staffing of agencies
Budget Paper No. 4 2026–27: Preface (external labour conversions)
National, state and territory population
series: Estimated resident population, Australia, June 2022 and June 2025 (benchmark computed automatically)

metrics.method: APS headcount (ongoing + non-ongoing) from APSC data at 30 June. The population benchmark is the change in ABS estimated resident population between the June quarters of the same years, computed automatically from the ABS Data API.

explainer.what: The Australian Public Service is the federal bureaucracy: departments and agencies such as Services Australia, the ATO and Home Affairs. It does not include the military, state public servants, or staff of government businesses.
explainer.why: Every public servant is paid by taxpayers. Growth can mean better services, or more administration, regulation and cost. We compare it with population growth to see whether the bureaucracy is growing faster than the country it serves.

metrics.title: NDIS cost growth
metrics.question: Is the government meeting its own target to rein in NDIS cost growth?

headline.caption: annual growth in NDIS costs

metrics.status_rule: Off track if annual NDIS cost growth is above the 8% growth target agreed by National Cabinet.
context: NDIS expenses rose from $28.6 billion in 2021–22 to $46.5 billion in 2024–25, and were $50.2 billion in the 12 months to March 2026.
The government's own impact analysis says the 8% target 'would not be met by July 2026'. A new target of 5–6% growth was set in January 2026.
The 2026–27 Budget puts NDIS expenses at $56.1 billion, including state contributions. The scheme supports 774,456 participants (March 2026).

sources.title: NDIS Reforms Impact Analysis (1 July 2026 update)

metrics.method: Scheme expenses by financial year from the Department of Finance estimates brief. Latest 12-month growth and participant numbers from the NDIS Reforms Impact Analysis.

explainer.what: The National Disability Insurance Scheme funds support for Australians with permanent and significant disability. It is jointly funded by the Commonwealth and the states and is now one of the largest items in the Budget.
explainer.why: Governments agreed the scheme's cost growth must slow to be sustainable. Missing the target means a larger share of taxes goes to one program, and less to everything else.

metrics.title: Net overseas migration
metrics.question: How fast is migration adding to demand for housing and services?

headline.caption: net overseas migration

metrics.status_rule: Off track if annual net overseas migration is more than 10% above the pre-COVID decade average; watch if above average.
context: 1,414,400 people have been added through net overseas migration since July 2022.
In the year to December quarter 2025 Australia's population grew by 412,500 while 172,642 new homes were completed: 2.4 new residents for every new home.
Net overseas migration was 538,341 in 2022–23 and 429,162 in 2023–24. In 2024–25 it was 302,184, about 52,000 above the 250,000 the government forecast in December 2023.

sources.title: Building Activity, Australia
series: Dwelling units completed, new residential, all sectors, original

metrics.method: Sum of the latest four quarters of ABS net overseas migration. Pre-COVID benchmark is the average of financial-year totals 2009–10 to 2018–19. Population growth is the change in estimated resident population over the same 12 months.

explainer.what: Net overseas migration is the number of people arriving to live in Australia (for at least 12 of the next 16 months), minus residents leaving on the same basis. It includes students, workers and permanent migrants. ABS data, summed over the latest 12 months.
explainer.why: Migration drives population growth, which adds to demand for housing, roads, hospitals and schools. We compare it with the pre-COVID average and with how many homes are being built.

promise.quote: We expect net overseas migration to halve next year.
promise.attribution: Treasurer Jim Chalmers, 14 December 2023. MYEFO 2023–24 forecast 250,000 for 2024–25.

metrics.title: Defence spending
metrics.question: Is Australia spending enough on defence in a more dangerous region?

headline.caption: of GDP on defence (traditional budget measure)

benchmark.label: Level the US has asked Australia to reach

metrics.status_rule: Off track if defence funding is below 3.5% of GDP, the level the US Defense Secretary asked Australia to reach 'as soon as possible' in 2025 and the core defence benchmark NATO allies adopted in 2025.
context: On the traditional budget measure, defence funding was 1.98% of GDP in 2021–22, 2.03% in 2024–25, and is 2.02% in 2026–27 ($62.6 billion).
In April 2026 the government said defence spending would reach 3% of GDP by 2033 'under the NATO approach', which counts more items than the traditional measure.
In June 2025 the Pentagon said Australia should increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP 'as soon as possible'.

chart.note: Budget-time figures as reported by defence analysts (2025–26 estimated actual; 2026–27 budget). Traditional appropriation measure.

sources.title: Defence budget 2026–27: the $14 billion disappearing act
2026 National Defence Strategy and Integrated Investment Program
Australia should surge defense spending to 3.5% of GDP, Pentagon says

metrics.method: Defence funding as a share of GDP on the traditional budget appropriation measure, as calculated and reported by defence budget analysts at each Budget. Defence's own budget statements publish dollars only.

explainer.what: How much the Commonwealth spends on the Australian Defence Force and the Department of Defence, as a share of the economy. Figures vary by method: the 'NATO approach' counts extra items such as some veterans' and security spending.
explainer.why: Allies and defence analysts have warned that Australia's strategic environment is the most dangerous in decades. Spending as a share of GDP is the standard way to compare commitment over time and across countries.

metrics.title: Laws passed
metrics.question: How much legislation has Parliament passed under this government?

headline.caption: Acts of Parliament passed in the government's first term

metrics.status_rule: Context only: the number of laws passed is not in itself good or bad, so this measure is not rated.
context: The 47th Parliament passed 354 Acts, against 407 in the 46th Parliament and 402 in the 45th.
Since the 48th Parliament opened on 22 July 2025, 133 Acts have received assent (to 11 September 2026).

chart.note: Acts assented, counted from the Federal Register of Legislation by assent date.

sources.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation (Office of Parliamentary Counsel)
sources.title: Acts collection: search by year of assent

metrics.method: Count of Acts in the Federal Register of Legislation by assent date within each Parliament's term. Cross-checked against the Parliamentary Education Office's 47th Parliament statistics (355 bills passed both houses).

explainer.what: The number of Acts, laws passed by both houses of Parliament and given Royal Assent, in each term of Parliament.
explainer.why: More laws aren't automatically better. This gives context on how busy the legislative agenda has been. Each new law typically needs public servants to administer it and imposes compliance obligations on the community.
